title: India's AI Reckoning: Middle Managers Face Mass Displacement as Companies Flatten Hierarchies
excerpt: From TCS to Oracle, Indian and global firms are eliminating mid-level roles as AI agents replace the coordination work that once justified the managerial layer.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • TCS cut 12,000 jobs in FY26, mainly in middle management, citing AI's impact on hiring.
  • Gartner predicts 20% of organizations will use AI to eliminate over half of middle management by 2026.
  • Ciel HR forecasts a 25-30% reduction in junior-to-middle management roles in India over the next four years.
  • Indian IT firms are shifting from labor arbitrage to capability arbitrage, redefining roles around AI collaboration.

The Middle Rung Collapses

For three decades, India's corporate ladder offered a reliable trajectory: enter at the bottom, ascend through middle management, and eventually reach the executive suite. Artificial intelligence is dismantling that pathway, and the consequences are reverberating across the country's most prized white-collar sectors.

At Tata Consultancy Services' annual general meeting last week, chairman N. Chandrasekaran was unequivocal. "Will it definitely lead to a decrease in hiring? Absolutely," he said. "The company will not be hiring the kind of numbers it used to hire—because certain portions of the work, in the current scheme of things, will go to agents." TCS, which employed just under 600,000 people at the end of March, retrenched roughly 12,000 in FY26, primarily in middle and senior grades, even as it made 25,000 offers to freshers for FY27.

The pattern extends well beyond TCS. Cognizant plans to cut approximately 4,000 jobs. Oracle slashed around 12,000 positions in India—part of 30,000 globally—to fund a multibillion-dollar AI infrastructure buildout. In the United States, 97,006 jobs were eliminated in May alone, with AI cited as the leading cause for three consecutive months, according to outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas.

Why the Middle Layer Is Most Vulnerable

"For 30 years, the middle layer existed because information had to move physically through people," explains Phil Fersht, CEO of HFS Research. "AI now does that synthesis directly, which means the core justification for the middle layer has been removed, not reduced."

Anshuman Das, CEO of recruitment firm Careernet, quantifies the exposure: professionals earning ₹16–40 lakh annually—those with six-plus years of experience—face the steepest risk. "The demand for lateral hires with six-plus years of experience has fallen by at least 25% for us in the last year," Das said.

"The sooner you start being the person who does the highest-value work in the room rather than the person who organizes who does it, the better positioned you'll be."

— Phil Fersht, CEO, HFS Research

From Labour Arbitrage to Capability Arbitrage

India's IT outsourcing model—built on low-cost, high-volume labour—is undergoing a fundamental redesign. Genpact, one of the industry's major players, has appointed a Global Agentic AI Officer, signalling the depth of the shift. The company's leadership has stated that the future of business process management lies in "outcomes, not labour," a philosophical pivot that reframes entire service lines around autonomous AI systems rather than human headcount.

Industry analysts describe this as the transition from "labour arbitrage" to "capability arbitrage"—where competitive advantage comes not from cheaper workers but from professionals who can design, govern, and orchestrate digital agents. New roles such as AI Workflow Designer and Agent Orchestrator are emerging, though their numbers remain far smaller than the positions they replace.

The Ripple Effect on Campuses and Careers

The disruption is reaching India's elite management schools. IIM Ahmedabad is developing an AI policy for students and faculty, and placement processes at several IIMs now test candidates on their ability to use AI tools effectively. "Firms are now benchmarking candidates using AI," said Viswanath Pingali, chairperson of IIM-A's placement committee.

The Shift in Management Roles
›20% of organizations to use AI for flattening structures by 2026.
›25-30% reduction in junior-to-middle management roles expected.
›New roles like AI Workflow Designer are emerging.
›47% of organizations still use traditional hierarchies.
›Only 13% expect to maintain traditional structures in three years.

The psychological toll is mounting. A study published in the US National Library of Medicine found that AI-driven job losses among Indian IT professionals produce "emotional shock, identity erosion, future-oriented anxiety, social withdrawal, and varied coping responses." Sabina Dewan of the JustJobs Network warns that even though less than 10% of India's jobs are in formal employment, these losses carry cascading economic effects.

What's Next

HFS Research data suggests 47% of organisations still operate in traditional hierarchies today, but only 13% expect to in three years. For India's millions of mid-career professionals—and the diaspora workers occupying similar roles in the United States, United Kingdom, and Gulf states—the message is stark: the managerial layer that once provided career stability and social mobility is being compressed, if not eliminated entirely. The question is no longer whether AI will reshape work, but whether workers can adapt before the restructuring is complete.
